blocks.text: On the dove's simplicity, gentleness, chastity and timidity.

Now, as we are about to treat of the habits of doves, we shall begin with the famous saying of Christ, Matth. X, 16. Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί [Ginesthe phronimoi hōs hoi opheis, kai akeraioi hōs hai peristerai]· Be ye prudent as serpents, and simple as doves. By Tzetzes, Chiliad 9, Hist. 263, φρόνιμοι [phronimoi] and ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] are taken as meaning the same thing. For after he has asserted that they are called prudent when, like serpents, they guard their head, that is, their faith in God, he immediately adds:

Ἀκέραιοι δὲ γίνεσθε, ὡς αἱ περιστεραί μοι· Καὶ τοῦτο πάλιν τὸ αὐτὸ δηλοῖ τε, καὶ σημαίνει. Ἀκέραιοι γὰρ λέγονται περιστεραὶ τοιώς δε, Φρόνιμοι, ὥσπερ λέγεται περιστερὰ τοῦ Νῶε. [Akeraioi de ginesthe, hōs hai peristerai moi; Kai touto palin to auto dēloi te, kai sēmainei. Akeraioi gar legontai peristerai toiōs de, Phronimoi, hōsper legetai peristera tou Nōe.]

But be ye simple for me as doves. And this again indicates and signifies the same thing. For doves are called simple, prudent in such a way as Noah's dove is spoken of. That is, the dove which returned to the ark, that is, to the church, from which one must not depart. Nothing more absurd could have been devised. For, like the serpent and the dove, so φρόνιμος [phronimos] and ἀκέραιος [akeraios] are in no way synonyms.
